source.title: Developing and evaluating human-led and large language model–assisted hybrid deductive–inductive workflows for qualitative analysis
source.journal: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association

atoms.canonical_statement: The study aimed to develop and systematically compare a human-led and LLM-assisted hybrid deductive–inductive workflow for qualitative analysis.
The study used a methodological comparison design in which LLM-generated thematic outputs were systematically compared with human-led analysis within a hybrid deductive–inductive approach.
Participants were adults with heart failure recruited from two outpatient clinics within a large, urban, academic health system in the United States.

atoms.canonical_statement: Research consultations were conducted either in person in a simulated clinical environment or by video visit and lasted approximately 20–40 minutes.
Personalized patient-reported outcome reports were reviewed collaboratively during consultations, and the consultations were not structured by a predefined interview guide.
After each consultation, research team members conducted reflexive interviews; consultation and interview sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and de-identified before analysis.
The analytic dataset contained 122 transcripts from 61 patients: 61 clinical consultations and 61 reflexive interviews.

population.label: Patients contributing paired consultation and reflexive-interview transcripts

atoms.canonical_statement: Human-led thematic analysis served as the reference analysis and was performed independently of and before the LLM-based analysis.

The human-led analysis used a hybrid deductive–inductive approach with a deductive framework informed by cultural health capital, chronic illness work, and patient data work/interpretive sense-making of patient-reported outcomes.

Human coding was conducted in Dedoose with iterative team review to refine the codebook and resolve discrepancies; thematic saturation was defined as continued coding yielding no substantively new themes.
LLM-based thematic analysis used ChatGPT Edu with GPT-5.2 in an institutional HIPAA-compliant enterprise environment, and all transcripts were processed within that environment.
Transcripts were processed in patient-level batches of five patients, comprising 10 transcripts per batch and approximately 20,000–30,000 words.
Preliminary sensitivity analyses comparing three-patient and five-patient batch sizes showed comparable thematic stability across the two configurations.
The LLM workflow used a structured eleven-prompt protocol and did not provide the model with the human-generated codes, codebook, or thematic structures at any stage.
For deductive coding, ChatGPT Edu received the same three conceptual articles used for the human reference analysis and generated a theory-informed coding schema that was applied to the transcripts.

After deductive coding, the model was prompted to identify additional inductive codes and themes not captured by the deductive framework, then synthesize batch-level outputs into themes with representative quotations.

For cross-batch analysis, thematic outputs from all 13 batches were uploaded simultaneously for dataset-wide synthesis; recurring cross-cutting themes were derived and classified as deductive or inductive.
The LLM workflow included two explicit human review points: batch-level theme review after Prompts 1–7 and cross-cutting theme review with quotation-fidelity verification after Prompts 8–11.

The eleven-prompt protocol sequentially confirmed transcript incorporation, developed a deductive framework, generated deductive and inductive codes, synthesized themes, compared themes across batches, generated cross-cutting themes, selected representative quotations, and classified thematic origin.
All 63 possible pairs formed by seven human-led themes and nine LLM-generated themes were evaluated for conceptual overlap using human consensus ratings and an LLM-based binary evaluation.

atoms.canonical_statement: Three human reviewers independently rated each theme pair as substantially overlapping, partially overlapping, or non-overlapping; majority agreement of at least two of three reviewers defined consensus, with discordant cases resolved by team discussion.

source_anchor.paragraph: Comparison of human-led and LLM-generated themes

atoms.canonical_statement: For LLM-based overlap evaluation, GPT-5.2 assigned each theme pair a binary overlap value in an independent prompt session to avoid contextual carryover.

source_anchor.paragraph: Comparison of human-led and LLM-generated themes

atoms.canonical_statement: Jaccard similarity was defined as the proportion of all 63 theme pairs judged overlapping, and Hit Rate as the proportion of human-led themes with at least one overlapping LLM-generated theme.

Representative quotations from batch-level and cross-batch analyses were manually checked against original transcripts and classified as verbatim, truncated, paraphrased reconstruction, partial hallucination, or full hallucination; theme–quotation support was also assessed.

Robustness testing used three five-patient batches (15 patients; 30 transcripts) across three runs: the original 1-2-3 batch order in December 2025, the same order in May 2026, and a 3-1-2 order in May 2026.
Among 61 participants, mean age was 60.8 years (SD 12.9); 55.7% were male; 45.9% identified as White, 29.5% as Black or African American, and 36.1% as Hispanic.

atoms.canonical_statement: Two substantially overlapping human–LLM theme pairs were consolidated into “Illness Management as Ongoing Work” and “Social and Contextual Resources in Illness Management.”

atoms.canonical_statement: The final integrated framework contained 14 themes organized into three domains: Illness Experience and Identity; PRO Data and Reports; and Clinical Relationships and Social Context.

source_anchor.paragraph: Comparison and integration of human-led and LLM-generated themes

atoms.canonical_statement: The integrated “Illness Experience and Identity” domain comprised Illness Management as Ongoing Work, Illness Experiences, Moral Framing of Self-Management, Agency Within Constraint, Calibration and Negotiation Between Body, Guidelines, and Lived Reality, Integration of Illness Into Identity and Normalcy, and Uncertainty as a Persistent Condition of Living.

The integrated “Patient-reported outcome Data and Reports” domain comprised Data Work; Data, Metrics, and Visual Reports as Identity-Shaping Tools; PRO Results Discussion; Perceptions, Reactions, and Preferences for PROs; and Uses of PRO by Patients and Clinicians.
The integrated “Clinical Relationships and Social Context” domain comprised Relational Recognition and Trust in Care Encounters and Social and Contextual Resources in Illness Management.
The LLM cross-cutting theme “Chronic Illness as Continuous, Structured Work” recurred in 10 of 13 independent analytic batches.

atoms.canonical_statement: All nine LLM-generated cross-cutting themes showed a similar pattern of recurrence across independent batches.
The LLM labeled six of nine cross-cutting themes as inductive and three as deductive.

Research-team review agreed that all three LLM-labeled deductive themes were deductive but reclassified five of the six LLM-labeled inductive themes as deductive because they closely matched a priori framework constructs.
After research-team review, eight of nine LLM-generated themes were judged deductive/framework-derived and only “Moral Framing of Self-Management” was judged genuinely inductive.
Seven of nine representative quotations supporting cross-cutting themes were reproduced verbatim.

atoms.canonical_statement: Verbatim quotation fidelity did not guarantee thematic support; some excerpts supported their assigned themes only indirectly or required additional interpretation.
The quotation “Sometimes I do have to take a nap” (REF76), although assigned to Integration of Illness Into Identity and Normalcy, did not by itself fully convey the meaning of that theme.
Across the three robustness runs, the labels and number of LLM-generated themes varied for each batch.

source_anchor.paragraph: Reproducibility of LLM-generated themes across runs

atoms.canonical_statement: Despite run-to-run variability, five core concepts recurred across robustness runs: chronic illness management, balancing, identity, data work, and relational trust; not all themes were consistently identified.

source_anchor.paragraph: Reproducibility of LLM-generated themes across runs

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that combining human-led and LLM-generated analyses yielded a richer integrated thematic framework than either approach alone.

The authors concluded that the LLM captured meaningful thematic content but contributed mainly deductive themes; only one of nine cross-cutting themes was judged genuinely inductive after human review.

The authors concluded that LLM-based qualitative analysis can meaningfully support large-scale transcript analysis, including unstructured patient–clinician consultations and semi-structured interviews.
The authors positioned LLMs as analytic partners within intentionally designed, human-governed workflows rather than automated substitutes for coding and theme generation.

The authors recommended repeated analyses under identical prompt conditions, manual verification of representative quotations, systematic human review and team consensus, and complementary evaluation approaches to strengthen rigor and reproducibility.
The study evaluated only one LLM, ChatGPT, so findings may reflect model-specific characteristics rather than general properties of LLM-assisted qualitative analysis.
LLM-generated outputs were sensitive to prompt design and model stochasticity, so identical prompts could yield different outputs across runs or over time.
Robustness testing covered only three batches totaling 30 of 122 transcripts, limiting characterization of reproducibility across the full dataset.
The study used a single clinical population of patients with heart failure, limiting direct generalizability to other clinical contexts and qualitative data sources.
Because transcripts were de-identified and participant demographics were not provided to the LLM, the study could not assess whether demographics influenced LLM-generated themes or quotations.
